passages.t: Run the race with your eyes on Jesus
passages.happening:
“Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with endurance the race set out for us” (verse 1).

“Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God” (verse 2).

“Consider Him who endured such hostility from sinners, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
The picture comes from the games held in cities all over the Roman world. Runners stripped off anything that could slow them down, ran before crowded stands, and fixed their eyes on the finish.

‘A great cloud of witnesses’ means the people of chapter 11. They are not mainly spectators watching us. They are witnesses in another sense: people who have finished the race and whose lives show that it can be run.

‘Every encumbrance’ is any weight that slows a runner, even things that are not wrong in themselves. ‘The sin that so easily entangles’ pictures something that trips a runner and brings him down.

‘Run with endurance’: this is a long race, not a sprint. The word means staying under a heavy load without giving up.

Then the centre of it all: ‘fix our eyes on Jesus’. He is ‘the author and perfecter of our faith’. ‘Author’ means the pioneer who goes first and opens the way; ‘perfecter’ means the one who completes it. He ran the whole course himself. He ‘endured the cross’. Crucifixion was the death Rome kept for slaves and rebels, a death of public shame, and he ‘scorned its shame’, treating it as nothing compared with ‘the joy set before Him’. And he finished: he sat down at God's right hand.
passages.ot:
The psalms and prophets often speak of God's people as weary and of God giving strength to keep going: “But those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not faint” (Isaiah 40:31).

The shame Jesus bore was foretold in the songs of the suffering servant: “He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3). And in the psalm he prayed on the cross: “But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by men and despised by the people” (Psalm 22:6).

‘Sat down at the right hand’ is Psalm 110:1 once more, the psalm that runs all through this letter.
passages.asks: Run with your eyes on Jesus. Ask what weights you are carrying that slow you down, even good things. Ask what sin keeps wrapping itself around your legs. And ask what it would change today to look at Jesus, who finished the race through shame and pain, instead of at the length of the road.

passages.happening:
“In your struggle against sin, you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood. And you have forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons: ‘My son, do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord, and do not lose heart when He rebukes you. For the Lord disciplines the one He loves, and He chastises every son He receives.’” (verses 4-6).

“Endure suffering as discipline; God is treating you as sons. For what son is not disciplined by his father?” (verse 7). Those who receive no discipline are not true sons (verse 8).

“Furthermore, we have all had earthly fathers who disciplined us, and we respected them. Should we not much more submit to the Father of our spirits and live? Our fathers disciplined us for a short time as they thought best, but God disciplines us for our good, so that we may share in His holiness. No discipline seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it” (verses 9-11).
passages.hearers:
The readers had suffered, but none of them had yet been killed for their faith. The writer wants them to see their hardship in a new light.

‘Discipline’ translates a Greek word for the whole raising of a child: teaching, training, practice and correction. It is the word behind ‘pedagogy’, the art of teaching. It is more like the training of an athlete than the punishment of a criminal. The verb ‘trained’ in verse 11 is the word for exercise in a gymnasium.

In the ancient world, a father who took care to train a son was treating him as his heir. A child born outside marriage often had no claim on the family's inheritance, and might get little of the father's attention. So the writer turns that into comfort: the hardship you are going through, received in faith, is not a sign that God has rejected you. It is a sign that you belong.

The writer is honest about human fathers. They disciplined ‘for a short time as they thought best’. They did not always get it right. God's training is always ‘for our good’, and its goal is that we ‘share in His holiness’. And he is honest about how it feels: ‘painful’. The harvest comes later.
passages.ot:
Verses 5 and 6 quote Proverbs 3. In the Berean Standard Bible, which translates the Hebrew, it reads: “My son, do not reject the discipline of the LORD, and do not loathe His rebuke; for the LORD disciplines the one He loves, as does a father the son in whom he delights” (Proverbs 3:11-12).

In its own setting this is a father teaching his son wisdom. It says that God's correction is a sign of his love, as a good father's is.

The last line differs in Hebrews, which follows the Greek Old Testament: ‘He chastises every son He receives’, where the Hebrew has ‘as does a father the son in whom he delights’. Both say the same thing: God's training flows from love.
passages.hard:
Does this mean my suffering is God punishing me? And does it say that harsh treatment of a child is right?

No, to both. Hebrews speaks to believers who were suffering for their faith, and says God can use even that hardship as a good father uses training, to make his children strong and holy. It does not say that every pain is a penalty for some sin. The Bible refuses that reasoning. Job's friends insisted that suffering always follows sin, and God said they were wrong. Asked whose sin made a man born blind, Jesus said, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3). So these verses must never be used to tell anyone that their illness, loss or pain is God punishing them.

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body.

Nor do these verses approve of a parent who harms a child. The writer admits that human fathers disciplined ‘as they thought best’, and not always well. These words must never be used against a child who is being harmed. Abuse of a child is a crime. It is to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, not handled quietly inside a church. If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now. If you were harmed as a child, what was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault.

What if ‘Father’ is a hard word for you? Some readers had a father who was absent, or who hurt them. If your own father was not there, or did not show you love, this passage is not asking you to picture him. It is telling you what you should have been shown, and what God is. If what happened to you still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: God trains those he loves. Ask whether you have read your hardship as a sign that God has left you, when he may be shaping you. Ask what ‘harvest of righteousness and peace’ you hope will grow from it. And if your own father hurt you, ask God to show you the Father you should have had.

passages.t: Strengthen weak knees; see that no one falls short
passages.happening:
“Therefore strengthen your limp hands and weak knees. Make straight paths for your feet, so that the lame may not be disabled, but rather healed” (verses 12-13).

“Pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness, without which no one will see the Lord” (verse 14).

“See to it that no one falls short of the grace of God, and that no root of bitterness springs up to cause trouble and defile many. See to it that no one is sexually immoral, or is godless like Esau, who for a single meal sold his birthright. For you know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. He could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears” (verses 15-17).
passages.hearers:
The race picture continues. Tired runners have drooping arms and shaking knees. ‘Strengthen’ them. Make the path level, so that those who are already limping do not fall and get worse, but heal. The writer is thinking of the whole group, especially its weakest members.

‘Pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness.’ Peace looks outward to others; holiness looks upward to God. Both are worth chasing.

‘See to it’ is spoken to the whole church. They are to watch over one another, so that no one ‘falls short of the grace of God’, like a runner dropping out of the race. A ‘root of bitterness’ is a picture from Deuteronomy of someone who turns from God and poisons others.

Then Esau. Genesis tells how Esau came home hungry and sold his rights as the firstborn son to his brother Jacob for a bowl of stew. He traded something lasting for something he wanted that moment. ‘Godless’ here means treating holy things as common, as if God's promises were worth less than a meal. Later, when the blessing went to Jacob, Esau wept and begged his father, but the blessing could not be taken back.
passages.ot:
Verse 12 echoes Isaiah: “Strengthen the limp hands and steady the feeble knees!” (Isaiah 35:3). Verse 13 echoes Proverbs: “Make a level path for your feet, and all your ways will be sure” (Proverbs 4:26).

The ‘root of bitterness’ comes from Moses' warning: “Make sure there is no root among you that bears such poisonous and bitter fruit” (Deuteronomy 29:18), speaking of anyone whose heart turns from the LORD to other gods.

Esau's story is in Genesis 25 and 27. Jacob gave the stew “to Esau, who ate and drank and then got up and went away. Thus Esau despised his birthright” (Genesis 25:34). When Isaac's blessing went to Jacob, Esau cried, “Bless me too, O my father!” “Then Esau wept aloud” (Genesis 27:38).
passages.hard:
‘He could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears.’ Does this mean God refused Esau's repentance?

Many readers take it to mean that Esau could not undo what he had done: his father would not take back the blessing given to Jacob. The tears were for the lost blessing, and the thing could not be reversed. On this reading it is not a story about God refusing a sincere turning of heart. Others read it beside 6:4-6, as a warning that a settled despising of God's gifts can harden a person until they no longer truly want to return. These notes do not choose.

Esau's story does not end in Genesis 27. Years later, when Jacob came home afraid, “Esau, however, ran to him and embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him. And they both wept” (Genesis 33:4). He became the father of a people. Hebrews uses one moment of his life as a warning; it is not the Bible's last word on Esau, and it gives no one licence to mock him or his descendants.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Strengthen the weak knees, and watch out for one another. Ask who in your church is limping, and how you could make the path smoother for them. Ask whether there is a ‘root of bitterness’ growing in you. And ask what you are tempted to trade for something you want right now.

passages.happening:
“For you have not come to a mountain that can be touched and that is burning with fire; to darkness, gloom, and storm; to a trumpet blast or to a voice that made its hearers beg that no further word be spoken” (verses 18-19). Even an animal that touched the mountain was to die, and “The sight was so terrifying that even Moses said, ‘I am trembling with fear.’” (verse 21).

“Instead, you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. You have come to myriads of angels in joyful assembly, to the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven. You have come to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (verses 22-24).
passages.hearers:
The writer sets two mountains side by side. The first is Sinai, where God gave the law. It was a real mountain, ‘that can be touched’, and it was terrifying: fire, darkness, a storm, a trumpet, a voice so awesome that the people begged it to stop. Even Moses trembled.

The second is Mount Zion, Jerusalem's hill, but here it is ‘the heavenly Jerusalem’, the city of the living God. The readers have ‘come’ to it already, by faith, though not yet in full. Look at who is there: countless angels at a festival, God's people whose names are written in heaven, God the judge of all, the faithful who have died and been made perfect, and Jesus.

‘The congregation of the firstborn’ means God's people, all of them heirs, as the firstborn son was the heir.

‘The sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.’ Abel's blood, after his brother killed him, cried out to God from the ground for justice. Jesus' blood speaks a better word: forgiveness and peace.
passages.ot:
The scene at Sinai comes from Exodus 19 and Deuteronomy. God told Moses to set a boundary: “Whoever touches the mountain shall surely be put to death” (Exodus 19:12). “there was thunder and lightning. A thick cloud was upon the mountain, and a very loud blast of the ram’s horn went out, so that all the people in the camp trembled” (Exodus 19:16). The people said, “For this great fire will consume us, and we will die, if we hear the voice of the LORD our God any longer” (Deuteronomy 5:25). Moses' fear is told in Deuteronomy 9:19: “For I was afraid of the anger and wrath that the LORD had directed against you”.

Zion is praised all through the psalms: “like the peaks of Zaphon is Mount Zion, the city of the great King” (Psalm 48:2).

Abel's blood is in Genesis 4: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10).
passages.hard:
Is Hebrews saying that Sinai, and the Jewish faith, belong to fear, while Christians have joy?

No. Sinai was God's own meeting with his people. He came down to Israel in glory, gave them his law, and made his covenant with them. The fear was the right response to the holiness of God, and the writer says Moses himself trembled. And Zion, the other mountain, is also Israel's mountain, the city of Israel's God, praised in Israel's psalms. Both mountains belong to Israel's Scriptures.

The contrast is between two ways of coming to the same holy God: from a distance, behind a boundary, as at Sinai; or drawn near through Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant. And the very next verses warn that the God of Zion is no less to be feared: ‘our God is a consuming fire’ (verse 29). The warning is aimed at believers in Jesus.

For centuries some Christians used this letter, with other parts of the New Testament, to teach contempt for Jews and Judaism. That reading is false. This site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why.
passages.asks: You have come to Mount Zion. Ask whether you come to God as if from far off, behind a boundary, or as one drawn near by Jesus. Ask what it means that you belong to a festival crowd that includes the faithful who have died. And ask what ‘better word’ the blood of Jesus speaks over your life.

passages.t: An unshakable kingdom, and a consuming fire
passages.happening:
“See to it that you do not refuse Him who speaks. For if the people did not escape when they refused Him who warned them on earth, how much less will we escape if we reject Him who warns us from heaven?” (verse 25).

“At that time His voice shook the earth, but now He has promised, ‘Once more I will shake not only the earth, but heaven as well.’” (verse 26). ‘Once more’ means that what can be shaken, created things, will be removed, “so that the unshakable may remain” (verse 27).

“Therefore, since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe. ‘For our God is a consuming fire.’” (verses 28-29).
passages.hearers:
This is the last of the letter's five warnings, and it returns to where the letter began: God has spoken. ‘Do not refuse Him who speaks.’ The argument goes from lesser to greater one more time. If Israel did not escape when they refused God's word at Sinai, how much more serious to refuse him speaking from heaven through his Son.

At Sinai the earth shook. God has promised to shake everything once more, heaven and earth. Everything that can be shaken, everything made, will be shaken. What will remain is what cannot be shaken: God's kingdom.

For readers who had lost their property, been mocked, and were tired, this was a strong word. The world around them was shaking. The kingdom they were receiving was not.

So the response is gratitude, and worship ‘with reverence and awe’. The letter does not end its teaching with a comfortable word. It ends with the holiness of God: ‘our God is a consuming fire’. The same God who welcomes us through Jesus is holy, and he is not to be taken lightly.
passages.ot:
Verse 26 quotes Haggai, who spoke to the Jews rebuilding the temple after the exile: “For this is what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘Once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land.’” (Haggai 2:6). In its own setting it was a promise that God would shake the nations and fill his house with glory. Hebrews' wording, ‘not only the earth, but heaven as well’, differs a little, as the writer usually follows the Greek Old Testament, and it stresses the ‘once more’.

Verse 29 quotes Moses: “For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God” (Deuteronomy 4:24). In Deuteronomy it is a warning against idols: the God who loves Israel will not share them with false gods.
passages.hard:
‘Our God is a consuming fire.’ Should believers be afraid of God?

The Bible speaks of two kinds of fear. One is terror, the fear of a slave before a cruel master, and Christ came to free people from that kind of slavery (2:15). The other is reverence and awe, the deep respect owed to a holy God, and that is what verse 28 asks for. The two can feel alike, but they are not the same. A child can stand in awe of a loving father's greatness without being afraid that he will be cruel.

Fire in the Bible both destroys and purifies. The God who is a consuming fire is the God who burns away what is false. For those who refuse him, that is a warning. For those who come to him through Jesus, it is the fire of a love that will not leave them as they are.

Read the warning of verse 25 together with the welcome of verses 22 to 24. The writer is speaking to people he hopes will listen. The book page's part on the warning passages sets out how Christians read them.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Everything that can be shaken will be shaken. Ask what you have built your life on that can be shaken. Ask whether your worship has reverence and awe, or has become casual. And ask what gratitude would look like for a kingdom that cannot be taken from you.
